@AaronErhardt 

I bumped required version of Rust (MSRV) to `1.91.1` I didn't find policy for MSRV, so I may assume it should be fine for the next release, right? In case it is not and there are some distros or other reasons to stick to later versions or Rust, please let me know and I remove these changes from the PR.

[`gtk4-rs`](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs) [declares MSRV `1.83` in their README.md](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs?tab=readme-ov-file#minimum-supported-rust-version), but they actually use [`1.86` in `Cargo.toml`](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs/blob/main/Cargo.toml#L44).

Another thing about MSRV is that I noticed that there were earlier declaration of it in README.md, but then it has gone. I favor explicit declaration of MSRV in README.md, but WDYT? If you don't mind to have it in README.md I can add a section, similar how it is done in `gtk4-rs`.

LGTM. Fair modernization to comply the modern features.

The only concern I would have would be related to using nightly rust builds for CI, though if we're using that just for doc gen I see no major issues tbh.

Gues it is still good to get a review on this from the main maintainer.

I'm slightly concerned that using a specific nightly version could lead to an outdated toolchain as time passes and part of the idea is to test against the same version docs.rs is using, so I'd like to change that eventually. But that doesn't block this PR, it's already large enough as it is.

I'd say we're ready to merge once the MSRV badge is updated.

Thanks for the work on the PR and also for the review!

> I didn't find policy for MSRV, so I may assume it should be fine for the next release, right?

Yes, we've just been bumping the MSRV from time to time to match our dependencies. We kinda always expected our users to use a recent-ish Rust version.

> I favor explicit declaration of MSRV in README.md, but WDYT?

Technically, there is this badge: https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/blob/main/README.md?plain=1#L12

After merge of #798 we only hold by `winnow`

```sh

   = note: removed in 1.92.0; see <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/138907> for more information

```

To be precise it was [fixed on `main` branch since Sep 29 2025](https://github.com/winnow-rs/winnow/commit/f218f4ae7ae9d079e52014b7f4a242cff9da89d4), but new version of `winnow` has not been released yet. So, the version we use 0.7.13 still holds `doc_auto_cfg`.

So, we need to pin `nightly` to `2025-09-27` version for doc generation. Once new version released and we switched to it we can return back to latest `nightly`.

Please, see a bit more details about that change in the [commit message](https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/pull/800/commits/26b539d3156cb4b1028ae369e7a8207266080fe4).

It also raised some questions in [`winnow` issue discussion](https://github.com/winnow-rs/winnow/issues/835#issuecomment-3560875092).

I assume through feature flag of `glib` or `glib-sys`. I investigated the issue a bit.

Currently our [CI relies on `ubuntu-latest` runner](https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/blob/main/.github/workflows/rust.yml#L73) which is ATM [Ubuntu 24.04](https://github.com/actions/runner-images?tab=readme-ov-file#available-images). It contains glib version `2.80`, hence incompatibility.

I'm running Debian Trixie (13.2) which contains glib `2.84.4`:
```sh
$ pkg-config --modversion glib-2.0
2.84.4
```

I tried `docs` job (`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings --cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly-2025-09-27 doc --all-features`) on my Debian and it has succeeded. So, apparently this is the last thing that holds our CI from green status ATM.

We have several options:
- Run our own runner with Debian `trixie` or Ubuntu 25.10. It requires self-hosted runner, so I assume it is not an option.
- We try to rollback some of dependency updates to get back to versions which requires only `2.80` of `glib`.
- We live with broken CI and wait for 26.04 of Ubuntu and then when it becomes new `ubuntu-latest` and our CI should be fix itself. Disadvantage: another half-year or more without green CI.

To me it seems like rollback of some upgrades would be the most feasible option, WDYT? I haven't tried it and it probably will be a bit involving, but I can try to that in scope of current PR.
I don't know the specific reasons for this, but the change makes sense.

> Run our own runner with Debian trixie or Ubuntu 25.10. It requires self-hosted runner, so I assume it is not an option.

We already have our own container image: https://github.com/Relm4/docs/actions/workflows/container_image.yml

It's probably an oversight that other jobs use it, but the docs job doesn't: https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/blob/main/.github/workflows/rust.yml#L16

Can you try adding this image to the docs job?

> What do you think about using it in our docs job?

In general, the idea is to match the build environment of docs.rs as closely as possible because you don't want to publish a crate and then see that it is not able to generate docs.

Actually, I just found this: https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs

Maybe this is a better solution?

I think we should merge this now though, since it is already large enough and keep those changes for another PR. What do you think?
@AaronErhardt May be you can take a look at #802 as a follow up as it's relatively small we can merge it as well you generally not against the idea.
Thanks for all your efforts :)

> Thanks for all your efforts :)

My pleasure!

future_requirement_candidates.text:
Hey everyone,

I'd be happy to help maintain Relm4 too. I'd be able to help with bug reports and dependency updates, but I'd also be open to adding some new features or resolving long-standing feature requests.

There are a few issues in Relm4 that require some sort of hard decision to be made. For example, [this `icons` pull request](https://github.com/Relm4/icons/pull/29). It seems to solve the issue addressed, but it'd be a breaking change for existing apps. Should this be merged, should some other approach be taken, or should the bug be left unaddressed and the PR closed? The PR already exists and is ready to merge -- the hard part isn't the code, but actually making the decision. Allowing the PR to sit unaddressed doesn't get us closer to any of these outcomes. (Please don't take this as a way of saying "you're not doing enough unpaid labour for me", I more mean it as "I'm willing to help reach a consensus". Even the Rust project has issues and PRs that sit open for years because, even though the code is done, the decision-making process takes a long time!)

Relatively uncontroversial changes, like updating dependencies or fixing typos, can easily be handled, but anything that requires a breaking change or a different approach will need some discussion. After all, anyone who has write access to the Relm4 icons repository could merge the aforementioned pull request right now, but would that be the right choice?

Along with general maintenance, I'd be willing to help out in getting these discussions moving.

@AaronErhardt 

I bumped required version of Rust (MSRV) to `1.91.1` I didn't find policy for MSRV, so I may assume it should be fine for the next release, right? In case it is not and there are some distros or other reasons to stick to later versions or Rust, please let me know and I remove these changes from the PR.

[`gtk4-rs`](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs) [declares MSRV `1.83` in their README.md](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs?tab=readme-ov-file#minimum-supported-rust-version), but they actually use [`1.86` in `Cargo.toml`](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs/blob/main/Cargo.toml#L44).

Another thing about MSRV is that I noticed that there were earlier declaration of it in README.md, but then it has gone. I favor explicit declaration of MSRV in README.md, but WDYT? If you don't mind to have it in README.md I can add a section, similar how it is done in `gtk4-rs`.

LGTM. Fair modernization to comply the modern features.

I assume through feature flag of `glib` or `glib-sys`. I investigated the issue a bit.

Currently our [CI relies on `ubuntu-latest` runner](https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/blob/main/.github/workflows/rust.yml#L73) which is ATM [Ubuntu 24.04](https://github.com/actions/runner-images?tab=readme-ov-file#available-images). It contains glib version `2.80`, hence incompatibility.

I'm running Debian Trixie (13.2) which contains glib `2.84.4`:
```sh
$ pkg-config --modversion glib-2.0
2.84.4
```

I tried `docs` job (`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings --cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly-2025-09-27 doc --all-features`) on my Debian and it has succeeded. So, apparently this is the last thing that holds our CI from green status ATM.

We have several options:
- Run our own runner with Debian `trixie` or Ubuntu 25.10. It requires self-hosted runner, so I assume it is not an option.
- We try to rollback some of dependency updates to get back to versions which requires only `2.80` of `glib`.
- We live with broken CI and wait for 26.04 of Ubuntu and then when it becomes new `ubuntu-latest` and our CI should be fix itself. Disadvantage: another half-year or more without green CI.

To me it seems like rollback of some upgrades would be the most feasible option, WDYT? I haven't tried it and it probably will be a bit involving, but I can try to that in scope of current PR.
I don't know the specific reasons for this, but the change makes sense.

> Run our own runner with Debian trixie or Ubuntu 25.10. It requires self-hosted runner, so I assume it is not an option.

We already have our own container image: https://github.com/Relm4/docs/actions/workflows/container_image.yml

It's probably an oversight that other jobs use it, but the docs job doesn't: https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/blob/main/.github/workflows/rust.yml#L16

Can you try adding this image to the docs job?

> What do you think about using it in our docs job?

In general, the idea is to match the build environment of docs.rs as closely as possible because you don't want to publish a crate and then see that it is not able to generate docs.

Actually, I just found this: https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs

Maybe this is a better solution?

I think we should merge this now though, since it is already large enough and keep those changes for another PR. What do you think?
@AaronErhardt May be you can take a look at #802 as a follow up as it's relatively small we can merge it as well you generally not against the idea.
Thanks for all your efforts :)

> Thanks for all your efforts :)

My pleasure!

Regarding the warning in the view macro, I'm not sure what the best way is. Probably, we should figure out which part of the code generation is causing the issue (e.g. using `cargo expand`) and then generating an appropriate attribute to suppress the error or even optimize code generation. The macro code is a little bit complicated and it requieres sort of its own dialect of Rust, but every macro is organized nicely into separate `parse` and `codegen` modules, and for us on the latter should be of interest. Maybe you can spot an easy solution there.

I would like to help more, but as you already see with my late review, I'm quite busy ahead of Christmas, but I can probably do one more round of reviews before that and then during the holidays I have some more time probably.

@AaronErhardt 

I bumped required version of Rust (MSRV) to `1.91.1` I didn't find policy for MSRV, so I may assume it should be fine for the next release, right? In case it is not and there are some distros or other reasons to stick to later versions or Rust, please let me know and I remove these changes from the PR.

[`gtk4-rs`](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs) [declares MSRV `1.83` in their README.md](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs?tab=readme-ov-file#minimum-supported-rust-version), but they actually use [`1.86` in `Cargo.toml`](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk4-rs/blob/main/Cargo.toml#L44).

Another thing about MSRV is that I noticed that there were earlier declaration of it in README.md, but then it has gone. I favor explicit declaration of MSRV in README.md, but WDYT? If you don't mind to have it in README.md I can add a section, similar how it is done in `gtk4-rs`.

LGTM. Fair modernization to comply the modern features.

The only concern I would have would be related to using nightly rust builds for CI, though if we're using that just for doc gen I see no major issues tbh.

Gues it is still good to get a review on this from the main maintainer.

I'm slightly concerned that using a specific nightly version could lead to an outdated toolchain as time passes and part of the idea is to test against the same version docs.rs is using, so I'd like to change that eventually. But that doesn't block this PR, it's already large enough as it is.

I'd say we're ready to merge once the MSRV badge is updated.

Thanks for the work on the PR and also for the review!

> I didn't find policy for MSRV, so I may assume it should be fine for the next release, right?

Yes, we've just been bumping the MSRV from time to time to match our dependencies. We kinda always expected our users to use a recent-ish Rust version.

> I favor explicit declaration of MSRV in README.md, but WDYT?

Technically, there is this badge: https://github.com/Relm4/Relm4/blob/main/README.md?plain=1#L12

I'm running Debian Trixie (13.2) which contains glib `2.84.4`:
```sh
$ pkg-config --modversion glib-2.0
2.84.4
```

I tried `docs` job (`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings --cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly-2025-09-27 doc --all-features`) on my Debian and it has succeeded. So, apparently this is the last thing that holds our CI from green status ATM.

We have several options:
- Run our own runner with Debian `trixie` or Ubuntu 25.10. It requires self-hosted runner, so I assume it is not an option.
- We try to rollback some of dependency updates to get back to versions which requires only `2.80` of `glib`.
- We live with broken CI and wait for 26.04 of Ubuntu and then when it becomes new `ubuntu-latest` and our CI should be fix itself. Disadvantage: another half-year or more without green CI.

To me it seems like rollback of some upgrades would be the most feasible option, WDYT? I haven't tried it and it probably will be a bit involving, but I can try to that in scope of current PR.

explicit_requirement_candidates.text: @jameskerr I think we should back out the changes to models/Program then merge this.

On the zed side of things we avoid not having tests that introspect the contents of the ast since this is often subject to change. I think I'd just have a test here that looked for a parser error and verifies the error message- something like `put x :=`.

I've updated the display of parsing errors.

![CleanShot 2024-02-26 at 11 01 05@2x](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/assets/3460638/e123ecd5-1699-40a9-84c6-6f40ea389099)

When going over this PR on a Zoom earlier with @jameskerr I drilled down a bit on how this branch currently leverages:

> ...the "/compile" endpoint from the default lake which runs locally in Zui.

An ongoing concern I've had for some time is that as more users start to use remote Zed lakes they may encounter difficult-to-debug problems when their local Zui and the remote Zed service have some kind of language/AST incompatibilities. I'm sure there's multiple ways we'll go about addressing this over time (e.g., I assume stricter API versioning could help here) but I've always got my eyes open to ways we can improve incrementally in the meantime.

As @jameskerr confirmed, up until this change Zui has always depended on the local Zed parser that shipped with the app, so relying on the `/compile` endpoint of the Zed that shipped with the app would not be making things worse. However, it seems like we have an opportunity now to use the `/compile` endpoint for a remote lake when one is in use, since this has the potential to catch some of the difficult-to-debug problems I cited above. In brainstorming about possible down sides to doing this, the increased latency of calling `/compile` over the network (which might be a WAN) was the one we could think of, so I set out to quantify this a bit.

I set up an EC2 instance in AWS `us-east-2`, started a Zed lake service on it, and connected to it from my home desktop in SF. I made a branch based on the one in this PR to which I added a patch @jameskerr provided to call out to `/compile` on whatever lake the user is currently connected to ([diffs](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/compare/wasm-parser...wasm-parser-remote-compile)) as well as a timer to log how long the parsing step takes. After loading some sample data to both the local and remote lakes, I set out to test the experience with needing to parse some simple Zed (just `count()`) and some sophisticated Zed (the attached 164-line shaper [sample.zed.gz](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/files/14412259/sample.zed.gz)).

The summary of the findings:

|**Lake location**|**`count()`**|**`sample.zed`**|
|-|-:|-:|
|Local|~4 ms|~75 ms|
|Remote|~150 ms|~300 ms|

The video shows the user experience in terms of visible delay in the app:

https://github.com/brimdata/zui/assets/5934157/22b6d2cd-388a-4241-abf4-1f8d0eca8a05

My conclusion: I think the change is worth making. Yes, speed is important, but I'd argue that correctness in catching/reporting errors is even more important, especially as we start adding more features over time that actually might _change_ the contents of a pool. In terms of how I imagine remote lakes will be used, I'm guessing what I'm doing here with accessing a lake on the other side of the country will be less common, and users that do it will likely become accustomed to other unavoidable delays. I suspect more remote lakes will be "local" in nature, e.g., like our community zync users that I think are all in the same geographic region. Finally, if the observed latency gets to be a problem I could picture fancy optimizations we could do, e.g., have Zui compare what's returned by the `/version` endpoint in both the local and remote lakes and if they match it could use the local `/compile` for parsing (though I'm not advocating doing any of that right now).

@mattnibs: Do you have any opinions to add here?

I am fine with using the current lake for the /compile endpoint. I can change the order of some of these operations to improve the speed if I know we are going to loose between 150 and 300 milliseconds on parsing.

Also, would it be possible (or does this already happen?) to return the parsing error message and location information from the /query endpoint when you submit a bad query?

I could also parse the query async to improve speed. The only reason for parsing first is to prevent adding to the history stack an invalid query entry. However, I could be hopeful that it will work, and if it does not, remove the entry from the history stack.

I did some thorough testing to quantify the benefits from this opening statement above:

> I've added a more robust mechanism for the zui-player tests to wait for the correct set of results after issuing a query. Many of our flaky integration tests were due to this problem.

## tl;dr

My results indicate that these benefits are indeed observable. This should allow us to bring some of our e2e tests back into the mix in CI. A detour during that work also led to a better understanding of separate issue #3021.

## Details

The changes in #2954 included no longer running the tests in [pool-loads.spec.ts](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/blob/main/packages/zui-player/tests/pool-loads.spec.ts) in CI because the tests often failed there but consistently succeed locally. One of the ways it was known to fail is described in #2843, and much of that issue text is speculation about the root cause being a timing issue related to not waiting long enough for results to appear after issuing a query, i.e., the exact improvement in this PR @jameskerr speaks to above. Therefore I set out to quantify if I could observe an improvement in the reliability of the `pool-loads.spec.ts` tests in CI.

Right out of the gate I became distracted because `pool-loads.spec.ts` includes the `bad data displays an error message` test that has nothing to do with checking query results but, as shown in #2954, it's been shown to fail in CI more than any other. I therefore took a detour to study that, which led to opening #3021. Now that's understood, I've excluded that particular test from all study of CI improvements from _this_ PR, i.e., hoping to just observe improvements in the symptoms shown in #2843.

First I did a baseline set of runs in https://github.com/brimdata/zui/actions/runs/8087230620 which was based on recent tip of `main`, removed the test from #3021, and ran `pool-loads.spec.ts` in a loop. On the Ubuntu runner this chalked up 7 failures out of 709 runs before the job got canceled (presumably for running too long) and all of them looked like the #2843 symptom.

Since #2843 speculates that waiting longer for results to appear might make the problem go away, I did another set of runs in https://github.com/brimdata/zui/actions/runs/8087202682 that's just like the prior set except that I added a 5-second sleep timer to each test before checking for the results output. Indeed this made it through 513 runs before the job got canceled and saw only one failure, which had a slightly different look than the #2843 symptom. Perhaps there was some intermittent Actions infrastructure problem that made the runner really, really unhealthy? Not sure.

## Conclusion

Since these failure rates are already small and might be prone to repro flare-ups based on how Actions is behaving on any given day, they're always a little tricky to study, but the tests do seem to show the desired improvement. I'll mark #2843 as fixed by this PR. If #3021 is still not close to a fix by the time this merges, I may look at breaking off that remaining test into its own file so we can start running the other now-reliable `pool-loads` tests in CI. It also looks like I could then look at revisiting issues #2026 and #2504 since they both depend on being able to reliably check query results.

Between my research and discussions with the team thus far, there's a few ways I see to potentially address this.

1. The Zed lake service could be enhanced to allow for listening for incoming connections on both IPv4 `127.0.0.1` and IPv6 `::1`. However, the Zed Dev team is currently tied up with other priorities, so consensus was to shelve this approach for now.

2. We could have the `zed-node` client connect to the local Zed lake service directly via IP `127.0.0.1`. Indeed, many of the users in the comments of the Node issues I've linked to above seem to favor this approach, and it also was the approach favored by the Brim team when discussing this issue as a group. I've made a Zui branch [zed-lake-only-localhost](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/compare/main...zed-lake-only-localhost) where I've made the necessary changes to get the app working with this change and make all tests pass. While I was ready to move forward with this approach, after spending more time with it as a user, I'm not in love with how this surfaces `127.0.0.1` in the UI where it used to say `localhost`, as the latter seems more self-documenting of it reflecting a connection to a "local lake". Granted, I'm guessing our more technical users would still understand, and maybe our less technical users wouldn't need to care. But it gave me reason to pause.

![image](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/assets/5934157/48bbd6d6-ce14-432f-8267-d37fb5281e36)

3. We could attempt to restore the prior Node behavior. This seems to be the second most discussed workaround in the Node issues linked above and can apparently be achieved by setting [`dns.setDefaultResultOrder('ipv4first')`](https://nodejs.org/api/dns.html#dnssetdefaultresultorderorder). I've made a Zui branch [zed-lake-localhost-dns-order](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/compare/main...zed-lake-localhost-dns-order) where I've made the necessary changes to get the app working with this change and make all tests pass. Compared to the connect-directly-to-`127.0.0.1` workaround, there's a few things I like about it:

   * It's fewer lines of code.
   * It still shows `http://localhost:9867` in the UI.

I learned late in all this about [Happy Eyeballs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Eyeballs) (also discussed in the Node issues linked above) that seems like it would have the potential to be the cleanest solution. As I understand it, the client would attempt to connect using both IPv4 and IPv6 and hence should allow the client to still request a connection to `localhost` and ultimately still successfully connect to `127.0.0.1` even if it tries and fails to connect to `::1` as well. Based on what I've read in the [Node `v20` release notes](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/changelogs/CHANGELOG_V20.md), between the existence of the `autoSelectFamily` option of [`socket.connect()`](https://nodejs.org/api/net.html#socketconnect) and [`net.getDefaultAutoSelectFamily()`](https://nodejs.org/api/net.html#netgetdefaultautoselectfamily) defaulting to `true`, I had the impression that if we moved up to such a newer Node release this might "just work". However, I've made a Zui branch [happy-eyeballs](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/compare/main...happy-eyeballs) which I tested when running Node `v20.12.0` and still saw the same `ECONNREFUSED`. Maybe there's more to it than I think. I can see the `zed-node` client connection relies on `node-fetch` and there's an open issue https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch/issues/1297 and closed-without-merge PR https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch/pull/1326, so maybe the base support for Happy Eyeballs in Node is not adequate? I'm still early in understanding all this.

When going over this PR on a Zoom earlier with @jameskerr I drilled down a bit on how this branch currently leverages:

> ...the "/compile" endpoint from the default lake which runs locally in Zui.

An ongoing concern I've had for some time is that as more users start to use remote Zed lakes they may encounter difficult-to-debug problems when their local Zui and the remote Zed service have some kind of language/AST incompatibilities. I'm sure there's multiple ways we'll go about addressing this over time (e.g., I assume stricter API versioning could help here) but I've always got my eyes open to ways we can improve incrementally in the meantime.

As @jameskerr confirmed, up until this change Zui has always depended on the local Zed parser that shipped with the app, so relying on the `/compile` endpoint of the Zed that shipped with the app would not be making things worse. However, it seems like we have an opportunity now to use the `/compile` endpoint for a remote lake when one is in use, since this has the potential to catch some of the difficult-to-debug problems I cited above. In brainstorming about possible down sides to doing this, the increased latency of calling `/compile` over the network (which might be a WAN) was the one we could think of, so I set out to quantify this a bit.

I set up an EC2 instance in AWS `us-east-2`, started a Zed lake service on it, and connected to it from my home desktop in SF. I made a branch based on the one in this PR to which I added a patch @jameskerr provided to call out to `/compile` on whatever lake the user is currently connected to ([diffs](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/compare/wasm-parser...wasm-parser-remote-compile)) as well as a timer to log how long the parsing step takes. After loading some sample data to both the local and remote lakes, I set out to test the experience with needing to parse some simple Zed (just `count()`) and some sophisticated Zed (the attached 164-line shaper [sample.zed.gz](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/files/14412259/sample.zed.gz)).

The summary of the findings:

|**Lake location**|**`count()`**|**`sample.zed`**|
|-|-:|-:|
|Local|~4 ms|~75 ms|
|Remote|~150 ms|~300 ms|

The video shows the user experience in terms of visible delay in the app:

https://github.com/brimdata/zui/assets/5934157/22b6d2cd-388a-4241-abf4-1f8d0eca8a05

My conclusion: I think the change is worth making. Yes, speed is important, but I'd argue that correctness in catching/reporting errors is even more important, especially as we start adding more features over time that actually might _change_ the contents of a pool. In terms of how I imagine remote lakes will be used, I'm guessing what I'm doing here with accessing a lake on the other side of the country will be less common, and users that do it will likely become accustomed to other unavoidable delays. I suspect more remote lakes will be "local" in nature, e.g., like our community zync users that I think are all in the same geographic region. Finally, if the observed latency gets to be a problem I could picture fancy optimizations we could do, e.g., have Zui compare what's returned by the `/version` endpoint in both the local and remote lakes and if they match it could use the local `/compile` for parsing (though I'm not advocating doing any of that right now).

@mattnibs: Do you have any opinions to add here?

I am fine with using the current lake for the /compile endpoint. I can change the order of some of these operations to improve the speed if I know we are going to loose between 150 and 300 milliseconds on parsing.

Also, would it be possible (or does this already happen?) to return the parsing error message and location information from the /query endpoint when you submit a bad query?

I could also parse the query async to improve speed. The only reason for parsing first is to prevent adding to the history stack an invalid query entry. However, I could be hopeful that it will work, and if it does not, remove the entry from the history stack.

I did some thorough testing to quantify the benefits from this opening statement above:

> I've added a more robust mechanism for the zui-player tests to wait for the correct set of results after issuing a query. Many of our flaky integration tests were due to this problem.

## tl;dr

My results indicate that these benefits are indeed observable. This should allow us to bring some of our e2e tests back into the mix in CI. A detour during that work also led to a better understanding of separate issue #3021.

## Details

The changes in #2954 included no longer running the tests in [pool-loads.spec.ts](https://github.com/brimdata/zui/blob/main/packages/zui-player/tests/pool-loads.spec.ts) in CI because the tests often failed there but consistently succeed locally. One of the ways it was known to fail is described in #2843, and much of that issue text is speculation about the root cause being a timing issue related to not waiting long enough for results to appear after issuing a query, i.e., the exact improvement in this PR @jameskerr speaks to above. Therefore I set out to quantify if I could observe an improvement in the reliability of the `pool-loads.spec.ts` tests in CI.

Right out of the gate I became distracted because `pool-loads.spec.ts` includes the `bad data displays an error message` test that has nothing to do with checking query results but, as shown in #2954, it's been shown to fail in CI more than any other. I therefore took a detour to study that, which led to opening #3021. Now that's understood, I've excluded that particular test from all study of CI improvements from _this_ PR, i.e., hoping to just observe improvements in the symptoms shown in #2843.

First I did a baseline set of runs in https://github.com/brimdata/zui/actions/runs/8087230620 which was based on recent tip of `main`, removed the test from #3021, and ran `pool-loads.spec.ts` in a loop. On the Ubuntu runner this chalked up 7 failures out of 709 runs before the job got canceled (presumably for running too long) and all of them looked like the #2843 symptom.

Since #2843 speculates that waiting longer for results to appear might make the problem go away, I did another set of runs in https://github.com/brimdata/zui/actions/runs/8087202682 that's just like the prior set except that I added a 5-second sleep timer to each test before checking for the results output. Indeed this made it through 513 runs before the job got canceled and saw only one failure, which had a slightly different look than the #2843 symptom. Perhaps there was some intermittent Actions infrastructure problem that made the runner really, really unhealthy? Not sure.

    > 120 |     await fields.waitFor();
          |                  ^
      121 |     let results = await fields.evaluateAll<string[], HTMLElement>((nodes) =>
      122 |       nodes.map((n) => n.innerText.trim())
      123 |     );
        at TestApp.getViewerResults (/home/runner/work/zui/zui/packages/zui-player/helpers/test-app.ts:120:18)

    - Expected  - 1

      Array [
        "this",

      ]
      39 |     await app.sleep(5);

```

Then for the big money, I did the set of runs in https://github.com/brimdata/zui/actions/runs/8087979145 which loops the test when starting from the branch in this PR, and there's no sleep timers. That made it through 655 runs on Ubuntu in CI and saw _zero_ failures.

## Conclusion

Since these failure rates are already small and might be prone to repro flare-ups based on how Actions is behaving on any given day, they're always a little tricky to study, but the tests do seem to show the desired improvement. I'll mark #2843 as fixed by this PR. If #3021 is still not close to a fix by the time this merges, I may look at breaking off that remaining test into its own file so we can start running the other now-reliable `pool-loads` tests in CI. It also looks like I could then look at revisiting issues #2026 and #2504 since they both depend on being able to reliably check query results.

Re: the design change back to commits and `_inner` functions:

The guard committed on `Drop` by holding `&mut` to the tracker, which worked while the tracker was a field on `Tunnel` next to the role state. Once the tracker moved into `GatewayState`, the guard's borrow of `self.flow_tracker` blocks every `&mut self` call that actually processes the packet, so the guard couldn't stay as-is.

One thing we could do is make the guard borrow-free (like the original `CurrentFlowGuard(()`) and have its `Drop` move the finished `FlowData` into a thread-local queue that the tracker drains at the next `begin_* / handle_timeout / close_all`. That gets rid of the _inner wrappers again, at the cost of the commit happening one step later and less visibly.

> I haven't tried it, but I assume driving normal async functions in a sans-I/O way is harder than driving `poll_*` functions?

This question is interesting! The two things are somewhat at odds in my view. A `Future` returns you `Poll::Ready` or `Poll::Pending`, so driving it manually means you gotta `match` on that return value.

There are reasons why you may want to do that, to e.g. drive a 2nd future concurrently (that is what `future::select` does). In the end though, encountering a `Poll::Pending` means you eventually need to return a `Poll::Pending` somewhere too!

The idea of sans-IO is that your protocol code should _not_ interact with `Poll`. Or at least not together with a `Waker`. `Option` and `Poll` have the same layout but they are semantically different. So whilst we could use `Poll` everywhere where we use `Option`, I think it may cause a bit of confusion at first? Or maybe this is actually a good idea?

```rust
fn poll_transmit(&mut self) -> Poll<Transmit> {
   Poll::Pending
}

For me, the importance of `&mut` can't be overstated. To me that's even more important than function coloring. To elaborate:

Maybe the most central concept in Rust, or the reason for it to exist as a language, is the borrow checker: which is all about the safe use of `&mut`.

In async code it's rarely appropriate to hold `&mut` references across an `.await` point to anything which isn't local to the task.

Thus in some respects async is at odds with the most fundamental part of Rust. 

Arc-Mutex, actors/channels, interior mutability all have their place, but async forces us to reach for them straight away. I think this often results in less good design and spaghetti code. 

Sans-IO allows us to structure the code in a lock free way by passing around `&mut` references – and it really brings out how great Rust is (sync Rust that is).

@thomaseizinger Turns out we were going about this completely the wrong way.

Adding a second app bundle means we need to embed _another_ copy of the network extension in that bundle in order to control it. This effectively creates two Firezone VPNs on the same system.

We could get around that by re-using the exact same bundle ID as the GUI app (this is the approach taken in this PR), but app store expressly enforces each signed binary to have a unique bundle identifier, so this build would have failed app store validation.

So the solution is... simply add a CLI interface to the main app 🙃. Seems obvious in retrospect.

We create a symlink `firezone-cli` pointing to the `Firezone` GUI app binary inside the bundle so that we can distinguish GUI launches from CLI invocations using `argv[0]`. No separate target, app bundle, entitlements, or any of that.

The api_key must be set
https://github.com/openai/openai-python/blob/15488ce07cb97535d8564e82dd5cda3481bc1a81/src/openai/_client.py#L97C12-L97C20
Anything using openai format needs the api_key to be not None
We should default it to an empty string or "dummy_key"

Isn't this checking if the key is valid? I think here we want to check if an API key has not been passed in (by any means) so we can prompt the user for one.

This change appears to instead check if 1) an API key isn't set in env vars and 2) a valid API key **is** set.

This is such a bizarre problem that I think stems from LiteLLM relying on OS env vars (which I encouraged them to do early on!) so we can never really know if an API key has been set.

I think we shouldn't expose `custom_llm_provider` to OI users— I'm happy to simplify / be opinionated on the fact that if an API base is set, it needs to be OpenAI compatible. My understanding of LiteLLM is that prepending "openai" to the model name simply sets the `custom_llm_provider` to OpenAI, but it's probably better to use `custom_llm_provider` under the hood so the model name is accurate. I like model being = "local"! Instead of "openai/x" or whatever we had before.

I'm happy to merge if this is minified to just set "custom_llm_provider" to "openai", in that place where we would otherwise prepend "openai/" to the model name, and set model to "local" if it's not already set (I'm also happy to do this).

I'll also talk to LiteLLM about letting us know when an API key isn't set (so we can pass a "dummy_key" like you suggest!).

`
['openai', 'custom_openai', 'text-completion-openai', 'cohere', 'anthropic', 'replicate', 'huggingface', 'together_ai', 'openrouter', 'vertex_ai', 'palm', 'gemini', 'ai21', 'baseten', 'azure', 'sagemaker', 'bedrock', 'vllm', 'nlp_cloud', 'petals', 'oobabooga', 'ollama', 'ollama_chat', 'deepinfra', 'perplexity', 'anyscale', 'mistral', 'maritalk', 'voyage', 'cloudflare', 'xinference', 'custom']
`

I was facing the same issue and updating to the latest version of chart.js resolved it. 👍 

Now I'm seeing more or less the same error, just from a different source:
```
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'save')
    at clipArea (helpers.canvas.ts:329:7)
    at Chart._drawDataset (core.controller.js:798:7)
    at Chart._drawDatasets (core.controller.js:772:12)
    at Chart.draw (core.controller.js:724:10)
    at core.animator.js:89:15
    at Map.forEach (<anonymous>)
    at Animator._update (core.animator.js:60:18)
    at core.animator.js:45:12
```

My chart uses `responsive`, but does not have a custom clip area defined; this seems to happen by default.

I'm a bit surprised that so few people are running into this issue.  Because I'm facing this in Vue 3 with a fairly simple bar chart that can be viewed in different timeframes triggered via buttons, which are then loading the requested data.  Is this use case so rare or are we (including the OP of this issue) doing something wrong?

For the time being, I'm working around the issue by reducing the animation duration from the default 1s to 250ms, in the hope that users are not switching between timeframes faster:
```js
{
  chartData: {
    options: {
      animation: {
        duration: 250
      }
    }
  }
}
```

> @LeeLenaleee, @etimberg This change broke my code. I'm using two x-axes to create an annotation effect with a bar chart: > > The annotation is the red bullet. A real world scenario would be to indicate that a bar is beyond a limit. I'm doing this by having a secondary x-axis on top of the chart area. To create an (optional) annotation I'm styling the tick label using a red bullet "⬤". This approach solved many other issues, e.g. you can easily hide the annotations by hiding just the secondary x-axis and it also frees space on the canvas when it's hidden by just the way Chart.js works. > > With this change my bars appear misaligned to the left. The reason is obvious as now two x-axes are counted and that alters the calculation of the bar positions in a bad in IMO unexpected way. I understand the intention of this PR but I'm also conviced the new behavior is a bug. Instead of grouping bars using multiple x-axes one should group using a group of bars instead: https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/samples/bar/stacked-groups.html. > > I can imagine this change will break other applications, too. For me, I either create another local patch to restore the previous behavior as now I cannot see any other way to implement this aside from creating a (complex) plugin. > > Edit: Or maybe we need a flag to indicate whether an axis should be counted. Creating this flag should be easy. But the question remains whether this is the right approach anyways or if one should just use groups of bars. We are experiencing the exact same problem

@etimberg maby best of we revert this change for now.

What do you think?

@liondog the stacked group has a different purpose, having different x-axis allows to display side by side different temporal data (i.e: comparison between 2024 and 2025, month by month) ; with stacked groups you won't have different labels (that why multiple axis are made for).
It seems to me that this bugfix is still justified and you used a bug as a feature ^^ Fixing a bug is always a kind of BC Break and I don't think that reverting this bugfix to use axis as annotations a good idea.

You probably may achieve the same behavior by:
- Adding a new dataset on the same axis for the red bullet
- Using the annotation plugin
- Listening `onClick` on the legend to programmatically disable the annotation if your secondary dataset is hidden

This implementation would be much more solid in my opinion

> @liondog the stacked group has a different purpose, having different x-axis allows to display side by side different temporal data (i.e: comparison between 2024 and 2025, month by month) ; with stacked groups you won't have different labels (that why multiple axis are made for). It seems to me that this bugfix is still justified and you used a bug as a feature ^^ Fixing a bug is always a kind of BC Break and I don't think that reverting this bugfix to use axis as annotations a good idea.

Thank you for giving more insights into your rationale for using two stacked timescales :-). It's a nice way of some sort of "line wrap" on one axis.

I wouldn't say that the previous behavior was a bug. That was, after all, the unchanged behavior of Chart.js for many years. I think both approaches are correct in their way. Perhaps your behavior could be extended to only count axes on the same border? Or on the same configurable "stack" (meaning a type of configuration that logically groups scales together, as implemented by this bug fix). Otherwise, what is the point of a second x-axis aligned to the _top_? Imagine another example with months being plotted on the bottom x-axis and quarters on another x-axis at the top of the chart to get a different visual grouping for the same bar dataset. This won't work anymore.

I will need more time to work out another possible solution for my use case, but for now I am fine with my patch. Your suggestions are not easily implementable as they introduce other problems.

To summarize: In my humble opinion, these two different approaches should be configurable.
